column3: “Jesus” supplies the unnamed subject; the Greek explicitly says “all His words.”
“The centurion” supplies the subject; the Greek verb means save or preserve.
“Just” is supplied, and the critical text uses “let my servant be healed” rather than a simple future.
The Greek gives the commands as direct speech and says “Do this,” rather than “do something.”
“The centurion” makes the Greek pronoun explicit.
“Jesus” supplies the subject; the Greek coordinates His disciples and the large crowd as going with Him.
“He saw” supplies a verb where the Greek introduces the funeral with “behold.”
The Greek term denotes a funeral bier, rendered as “coffin.”
The Greek says a prophet “was raised up,” rather than “has appeared.”
The Greek already places John’s calling two disciples in this verse; BSB moves it to verse 19.
The calling of two disciples is in the preceding Greek verse; BSB places it here.
The Greek uses the image of stumbling or taking offense, rendered as “fall away on account of.”
The Greek has present “I send,” rather than “I will send,” and explicitly retains “before Your face.”
“For” makes a causal link explicit where the Greek uses a participle describing their baptism.
